title: Why Your Students Need Breathing Room
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin critiques the common tendency of teachers to over-teach — talking too much, helping too much, and hovering too much — leaving students no room to think, create, or act for themselves. He argues this over-involvement produces needy, dependent students who stop relying on their own abilities and expect constant reteaching. It also breeds boredom, low motivation, and misbehavior, since passive students left unchallenged grow listless and prone to disruption. Beyond behavior, he says, over-teaching damages a teacher's ability to build rapport, since students grow tired of hovering and resent smothering attention. He calls for a '50/50' balance where teachers give their best in preparation and instruction, then genuinely step back and let students do the work themselves.
points: Over-teaching — talking, helping, and hovering too much — leaves no room for students to think, create, or act independently.
Constant teacher input creates needy, dependent students who lose confidence in their own abilities.
Passive, over-managed students grow bored and unmotivated, which directly increases misbehavior.
Excessive hovering damages rapport, since students grow tired of and resent a smothering teaching style.
Effective teaching should be a 50/50 proposition: give your best in preparation, then genuinely step back and let students do the work.
quotes: In an effort to be the best teacher they can be, most teachers over teach. That is, they talk too much, help too much, and are seen too much.
They don’t allow for their students to do for themselves, think for themselves, or create for themselves.
When you over-teach, your students become so accustomed to your input and guidance that they stop relying on themselves and their own abilities.
With you front and center—and everywhere in between—your students will get comfortably cozy being passive participants.
If your classroom is you-centered, if you’re in the habit of doing for your students instead of letting them do for themselves, then they’ll quickly grow tired of you.
Let your students do what you prepared them to do. Set them up for success. Check thoroughly for understanding. And then step back and observe.
